en: Regarding the *Rāstrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Sengyou’s catalogue states that Master Dao’an lost the name of the translator; it is now appended to the Western Jin records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a bodhisattva who was a great king named Jīvaka;
the king had a crown prince named Ajīva."

The King ruled the state with righteous governance; he did not inflict the suffering of swords or staves upon his officials or the people, and the winds and rains fell in their proper seasons as the five grains ripened in abundance.
There was a neighboring king whose rule was tyrannical and cruel; failing to practice correct governance, his subjects were impoverished.
He said to his attendants: "I have heard that the kingdom of King Dīrghāyu is not far from here; it is flourishing, prosperous, and joyful, yet it lacks military preparedness."
"I wish to go there to attack and seize their kingdom;
do you think it can be achieved? A minister replied, "Excellent!"
He then raised an army and marched until he reached the borders of King Dīrghāyu’s kingdom.

The officials and citizens on the border fled to inform the king, saying, "That King Lobha has raised an army and is coming, intending to attack the kingdom of the Wise King; we pray that you prepare for this contingency."
King Dīrghāyu summoned his ministers and addressed them, saying:
"The reason he has come is solely because he covets the people of my kingdom, the grain in our granaries, and our precious treasures."
"If we were to fight them, our people would surely be injured.
To contend for a state by killing its people is something I will not do.
The ministers said:
"Your subjects are all well-versed in the arts of war and shall certainly be able to defeat them, ensuring that the army of Your Majesty does not suffer incursions from the enemy.
The King said,
"If I am victorious over them, there will inevitably be deaths and injuries."
"Both those soldiers and our people cherish their own lives; to love ourselves while harming others is not the conduct of a wise man.
The ministers would not listen, and they detained the king within the palace. Thereupon, they themselves mobilized troops outside the city and went out to the border to confront and resist them.
The King of Long Life then said to his crown prince:
"He covets my kingdom and has therefore come to attack me.
Now, for my sake, the ministers wish to oppose and repel him."
"When two enemies face each other, there will inevitably be casualties; now I wish to abandon the kingdom with you and flee.
The Crown Prince replied, "I agree."
Thereupon, father and son together leaped over the city walls and went into seclusion among the mountains.
Subsequently, King Greedy entered that kingdom and issued a proclamation, offering one thousand *jin* of gold and ten million coins for the head of King Long-Life.
On a later day, King Dīrghāyu went out and sat beneath a tree by the side of the road.
A brahmin from a distant land arrived and also rested beneath the tree.
He asked King Dīrghāyu:
"Where are you from, sir?
For what reason are you here?
The king asked.
"I am a man from this kingdom of mine; I have merely come here by chance for amusement.
King Dīrghāyu asked the brāhmaṇa, "Worthy one, from where have you come?"
"Where do you intend to go?

The brāhmaṇa replied, "I am a poor and lowly practitioner from a distant land. Having heard from afar that the King of Longevity in this country delights in giving and provides universal relief to the poor and the weak, I have come from far away wishing to beg for alms so as to sustain my own life."
I do not know what the King’s intention is now;
you are a subject of this land, so having heard his intent, how do you find it now?
Are you willing to practice giving or not?
The king thought silently to himself:
"This son has come from afar for my sake; now that I have lost my kingdom, he will arrive with nothing to gain and must depart empty-handed."
"How deeply pitiable! Thereupon,
the king shed tears and said to the brahmin, "I am indeed King Dīrghāyu."
"A king of another state has come to attack me; I abandoned my kingdom and fled to hide here.
Now I hear that you, O worthy one, have come specifically to seek refuge with me. As I am currently destitute and lack the means to provide for you, what shall I do?"
The two men faced one another, sobbing and weeping.
The king said, "I have heard that the new king admires me most deeply; if you take my head to him, you shall receive a great reward."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have heard from afar that Your Majesty universally rescues all beings; therefore, I have come to beg, hoping to obtain a small amount to sustain my remaining life."
"Since Your Majesty has lost your kingdom, it is due to my own meager merit; now that you command me to have my head cut off, I dare not accept your order.
The king said, "You have come from afar with the intention of obtaining something, yet you have encountered my misfortune; I have nothing with which to satisfy you."
Furthermore, all those born into this world must eventually face death; since we ourselves shall die, we wish to offer our bodies as a gift—why should we refuse?
If you do not take them now, others will come later, and I would still give them to those people; it would be better to take them now.
The Brahmin said, "I cannot bear to kill the Great King.
If Your Majesty possesses such great compassion that you truly desire to sacrifice your life to grant it to me, then you need only release my hand and follow me."
The king followed him immediately; having reached the city gate, he ordered him to be bound and presented to King Greed.
King Greed then offered a reward of gold coins to the brahmin and sent him back.
"Then King Greed dispatched men to the crossroads to burn and kill King Long-Life.
Because of this, the ministers said to King Greed:
'This is our former lord who is now about to face the penalty of death; we pray that you permit us to prepare a modest funeral rite to see him off.'"
King Greed listened to this.
The ministers prepared a sumptuous meal, yet they stood before it with choked voices; the people who watched all said, "The king has died an unjust death."
In the cities, towns, fields, and wilderness, there was no one who did not cry out to Heaven.

When the Crown Prince Changsheng went out onto the roadside, he heard the people’s talk and learned that his father had been captured by the greedy king. He then feigned carrying firewood out to sell it in the marketplace, mingling among the noisy crowds.
Standing before his father, he beheld that his father was about to die and felt profound grief in his heart.
Seeing that Changsheng was present, the father feared that he might become enraged and seek vengeance on his behalf; thus, the father looked up to heaven and sighed deeply, saying:
"If one wishes to be a filial son of the highest degree, one must ensure that your father dies without resentment."
Do not seek to avenge your father; he would have preferred death and felt no anxiety.
If you were to disregard his words and kill another, it would leave your father with lingering resentment even in death.
Unable to bear the sight of his father’s death, Changsheng returned to the mountains; King Changshou was consequently executed by being burned alive.
After a long time, Changsheng thought to himself:
"My father was profoundly sincere in his benevolence and righteousness, never wavering even unto death."
Yet this King Greed is lawless and makes no distinction between good and evil, having unjustly put my father to death.
Although my father possessed a heart of compassion and profound benevolence and did not harbor resentment even in his dying moments, I cannot endure this.
If I do not go forth to slay this King Greed, I shall never again live a life of mere expediency in this world.
He then went out to seek employment.
A high minister of the state was advertising for laborers in the marketplace and hired Changsheng.
He had him plant vegetables, and the produce was excellent.
On a later day, the minister went to inspect the garden and fields; seeing that the vegetables were excellent, he called the garden supervisor and questioned him.
The supervisor replied, "I previously hired a man to tend them, and for that reason they are so fine."
The minister then summoned Changsheng; upon seeing him, he asked, "Are you somewhat capable of preparing food and drink? He replied:
"He can. He then prepared food and drink that were exceedingly sweet and delicious, and invited the king.
When the king went there to partake of the meal, finding the food and drink so sweet and delicious, he asked:
"Who prepared this food?
The minister replied,
"I previously hired a man who was able to prepare such food."
The king then summoned him and brought him back to the palace, ordering him to prepare food and drink.
On the following day, the king asked Changsheng,
"Have you already practiced the art of war?"
He replied, "I have indeed practiced it.
The king then took it and placed it by his side, saying to him:
"I have an enemy, the Prince Jīvaka.
I am constantly afraid that in my travels he might suddenly encounter me; now that we rely upon one another, I hope you will assist me in preparing for him."
Changsheng replied, "Indeed,
I shall exert my strength and offer my life for the sake of Your Majesty.
On a later day, the king questioned Changsheng:
"Would you perhaps enjoy hunting?
He replied, "Your servant has enjoyed hunting since my youth."
The king then issued an order to prepare the carriage outside and went out on a hunt together with Changsheng.

As soon as they entered the mountain forest, they saw running beasts; the king and Changsheng galloped after them, entering deeper and deeper into the mountains until they became confused and lost their way, unable to find the exit.
Having been lost for three days, they eventually reached a state of hunger and exhaustion. The king then dismounted from his horse, unsheathed his sword, and handed it to Changsheng, saying:
"I am utterly weary; you sit here, and I wish to rest with my head upon your knees."
Changsheng replied,
"Yes. Thereupon,
the king was able to lie down.
Changsheng thought to himself, "From the past until now, I have sought an opportunity to seize my son; today, at last, I have obtained what I desired.
He then drew his sword, intending to kill King Tan.
He reflected:
"When my father was on the verge of death, he charged me with earnest entreaties; how could I satisfy my own foolish desires and violate the final instructions of my compassionate father?"
He immediately withdrew the sword and desisted.
The King was startled into realization and asked Changsheng:
"In a dream, I saw Prince Changshou coming to kill me; I was greatly terrified."
"Why is this so? Changsheng replied, "In these mountains there are powerful spirits and ghosts; seeing Your Majesty here, they have come merely to terrify you."
"I shall personally attend to Your Majesty as your guard; you need only lie down in peace, for there is nothing to fear.
The king returned to his bed, but Changsheng again drew his sword, intending to kill him; however, remembering his father’s words once more, he desisted.
The king was again startled awake and said to Changsheng:
"I have once more dreamed that Prince Changshou intends to come and kill me; I am greatly afraid of him."
"Why is this so? Changsheng replied,
"It was simply the work of the mountain deity."
"The King has nothing to fear.

The King returned once more to his bed; Changsheng again drew his sword, intending to kill him, but reflecting on his father’s words, he desisted. He then cast the sword upon the ground, no longer harboring any intent to slay the King.
The King was again startled awake and said to Changsheng:
"I have once more seen Prince Changshou in a dream, who spoke of himself, saying:
'Grant me clemency.'"
"He will no longer kill me. Thereupon, Changsheng said:
"I am indeed Changsheng, the crown prince of King Changshou. I have come out for this very purpose, desiring to kill the Great King to avenge my father's grievance."
I reflect that when my father was on the verge of death, he earnestly entrusted me with this charge, not wishing for me to seek revenge;
yet, out of folly, I desired to disobey my father’s words. Upon careful reflection, however, his instructions were so sincere, compassionate, and urgent that I dare not transgress them.
Therefore, I now cast this sword to the ground to comply with my father’s words.
Nevertheless, I still fear that on a later day I might become confused and lose my way, thereby violating the instructions of my deceased father.
"I now therefore address you myself: I pray that Your Majesty will execute me immediately, so that this evil intent may be extinguished and severed from beginning to end.
The King then repented, saying:

"I have been a cruel and rebellious man, unable to distinguish between good and evil. These worthy father and son have practiced benevolence with such steadfast purity that they would not waver even unto death, yet I was greedy and harsh, never perceiving it at first."
Today it is thus; my life rests in your hands.
Because you have long cherished benevolence and remember your father’s words, you have not harmed me; this is truly a profound and gracious favor.
Now that I wish to return to my kingdom, by which path should I go?
Changsheng said, "I knew the path ahead, which is why I came; I have come to delude the Great King so that he may avenge his father’s grievance.
Changsheng then went out of the forest with the king and saw the ministers scattered all along the forest's edge.
The king then stopped sitting and prepared food and drink.
He asked his ministers:
"Do you know the prince Jīvaka, the son of King Jīvaka?"
Among them, those who did not recognize him replied, "I do not know him.
Among them, there were those who recognized him; having previously received the king's grace of longevity, yet fearing that the king might kill him, they also said:
"I do not know him.
The king then pointed him out and said,
"This is indeed Changsheng."
The king said, "From this day forward, I shall return to my own native land; I wish to entrust this kingdom to the crown prince.
From this day forward, you are my younger brother; should another kingdom come to invade and seize us, we shall provide mutual assistance."
The king then led his ministers and troops back to his own country, where they presented one another with rare and extraordinary treasures as gifts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The King Long-life at that time was none other than my own self."
The Prince Changsheng was Ānanda;
the Greedy King was Devadatta.
Devadatta has harbored enmity toward me life after life; thus, although I have directed wholesome intentions toward him, he nevertheless seeks to harm me.
Ānanda gave it to him without any ill intent; thus, upon meeting, they immediately felt a spirit of reconciliation.

The Bodhisattva sought the Way with such diligent hardship that even when confronted by those who would harm him, he harbored no heart of resentment or anger; therefore, he attained Buddhahood and became the Honored One of the Three Realms.
The bhikṣus rejoiced and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha is the master mariner of the ocean; he is the bridge of Dharma that crosses the river-ford, the carriage of the Mahāyāna path, by which all devas and humans are delivered.
He is also said to have untied his own bonds, crossed to the other shore, and attained the state of a transcendent immortal.
He has caused all his disciples to likewise untie their fetters and reach Nirvana.
Having come to pay respectful homage to the Dharma King, his mind rests in peace through the power of the Right Path.
The Most Victorious One is called Buddha; his fame is as manifest as the Snowy Mountains.
Like a pure flower, he is beyond doubt; to find joy in him is like being near a fragrance.
Ten thousand bodies gaze upon him without weariness; his radiance is as brilliant as a celestial luminary.
The Eightfold Right Awakening is self-attained; it is without departure and without defilement.
With craving exhausted, the net of desire is torn asunder; this is spontaneous, received without a teacher.
My practice has no master or protector; my resolve is solitary, without equal or peer.
By accumulating [merit], one attains Buddhahood; from this, one penetrates the holy path.
The ultimate path has no coming or going; it is profound, subtle, pure, wondrous, and true.
Neither perishing nor being born again—this state is Nirvana.
This essential tranquility is unsurpassed; ultimately, one shall not experience suffering.
Though the heavens possess auspicious realms, none can equal Nirvana.
My Teacher is the God among Gods, the Infinite Honored One of the Three Realms.
With the marks and signs, his body is sixteen feet tall; By means of supernormal powers, he travels through the void.
Perfumed by flowers, he removes the five aggregates; He uproots and severs the twelve sense bases.
Not coveting celestial or worldly positions, His mind is pure as he opens the gates of the Dharma.
The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma; his Way governs pure and equal conduct.
In future ages, the Three Jewels shall sever and extinguish all desires and passions.
Free from suffering, they attain the supreme state of non-action, ever joyful, blissful, and at peace.
May I always assemble before the Buddha, Equally delivering all living beings;
Following the fundamental practices and vows of the Buddha, I shall exert diligence for a hundred kalpas.
Through the four great equalities and vast giving, May the ten directions receive this great grace.
Maintaining precepts, pure and stainless, With loving-kindness and gentleness protecting all beings;
Entering meditative concentration through wisdom, And universally reciting the sutras with great compassion—
Thus one is always revered by the wise And honored as the foremost among the assembly of sages.
Śakra and Brahmā take him as their teacher; thus one knows the Buddha to be the most honored.
Hard to encounter and without peer, he is supreme and beyond compare.
As his merit spreads abroad, one should prostrate in worship to him.
Listen to my song of the ten directions: Casting off hindrances, one dwells in tranquil meditative absorption.
Light penetrates and illuminates the seven heavens; The fragrance of virtue surpasses that of sandalwood.
The Supreme Deity, wondrous and sublime, has come, Praising with reverence and desiring to behold the Honored One.
Śakra and Brahmā, with minds of equal reverence, bow their heads, desiring to receive his questions;
for the sake of the Buddha’s deliverance of the world, he bestows blessings everywhere.
The teachings and precepts he proclaims are clear and distinct in every place.
Furthermore, through the dissemination of the Dharma, disciples joyfully accept and practice it,
causing devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons to respectfully receive their prostrations with heads bowed.
*The Sūtra of King Cīrāyuṣa*
